summary.text: The seabed, also called the seafloor or ocean floor, is the bottom of the ocean.
Its structure is governed by plate tectonics, and from the deep abyssal plain it climbs toward the continents through the continental rise, slope and shelf.
Most of it is covered in layers of sediment that come from land, from living things, from chemical reactions and even from space.

items.prompt: Tiny plankton with hard shells die near the surface, and their shells drift down and pile up on the bottom. What kind of sediment do they become?

options.label: Terrigenous, made from land
Biogenous, made by living things
Hydrogenous, made by chemical reactions
Cosmogenous, made from space

items.explain: Sediment built from the hard parts of sea creatures, such as plankton shells, is biogenous.

items.prompt: A boat heads from a beach straight out to the deep open ocean. In what order does the bottom beneath it change?

options.label: Slope, shelf, rise, then abyssal plain
Rise, slope, shelf, then abyssal plain
Abyssal plain, shelf, slope, then rise
Shelf, slope, rise, then abyssal plain

items.explain: Going from shallow to deep, the shelf drops into the slope, then the gentler rise, and finally the abyssal plain.

items.prompt: Seafloor spreading pushes up a long underwater mountain range. Where does that range run?

options.label: Through the middle of the ocean basins
Along the edges of the continents
Only beneath the polar ice caps
Just offshore from large river mouths

items.explain: Seafloor spreading creates mid-ocean ridges along the center line of major ocean basins, between the continents.

items.prompt: In volcanic areas of the deep seabed, hydrothermal vents release something into the near-freezing water around them. What?

options.label: Cold fresh water from underground rivers
Streams of molten lava and gas bubbles
Very hot, high-pressure water and chemicals
Clouds of sand and plankton shells

items.explain: Hydrothermal vents release high-pressure, extremely hot water and chemicals into the typically freezing water around them.

items.prompt: A drilling crew labels a mud sample "120 mbsf". What does that number tell you?

options.label: How deep the water was above the bottom
How far down into the seabed it was taken
How far the ship was from the nearest shore
How many years the mud took to settle

items.explain: mbsf means meters below the seafloor, a measure of depth within the seabed itself, such as down a sediment core.

items.prompt: Why does so much of the world's plastic end up in the ocean, with some sinking to the seabed?

options.label: Ships dump nearly all of it at sea
Ocean water pulls plastic in from the air
Plastic is made mostly on the coast
The world's waterways all end up in the ocean

items.explain: The ocean is the final destination for global waterways, so much of the world's plastic ends up there and some sinks.

beats.title: Stepping Down to the Deep
beats.hook: The bottom of the sea is a staircase of shelves, slopes, ridges and trenches, dusted with sediment from land, sea life and even space.

beats.prompt: Put these parts of the seabed in order, from the coast out to the deep ocean.
beats.explain: From the abyssal plain the seabed climbs toward the continents through the rise, the slope and then the shelf, so walking out from shore you meet them in reverse.

beats.prompt: Sort each sediment by where it comes from.

left.label: Dust blown out to sea by wind
Plankton shells that sink after death

beats.explain: Terrigenous sediment is material eroded or blown off the continents; biogenous sediment is built from the hard parts of sea creatures such as plankton.

beats.prompt: Match each seabed feature to what creates it.

right.label: Mantle circulation from ridge to trench

beats.explain: Movements of the plates and the mantle build ridges, trenches and island chains, while falling sediment builds the gentle rise.

beats.prompt: Storm waves churn the water over a shallow coastal seabed. What happens to the sediment on the bottom?
beats.explain: In shallow water, tidal and wave energy resuspend seabed sediments, and currents carry them away.

choices.label: It hardens into solid rock right away
choices.feedback: Turning sediment into rock is not what waves do; they lift and move it.

choices.label: It is stirred back into the water and moved by currents
It sinks deeper, down into the mantle
choices.feedback: Waves act on the surface of the seabed, not deep inside the Earth.

choices.label: It stays put, since waves never reach the bottom
choices.feedback: In shallow water, wave and tidal energy do reach the seabed.

beats.idea: Plate tectonics shapes the seabed's steps and ridges, while sediment from many sources settles over most of it.

paragraphs.heading: The bottom of the ocean
paragraphs.text: The seabed is simply the floor of the ocean. People also call it the seafloor, the sea floor, the ocean floor or the ocean bottom. Its large-scale shape across the whole global ocean is set by plate tectonics. Most of it, in oceans all over the world, lies under layers of marine sediment.

paragraphs.heading: From the coast to the deep
paragraphs.text: Heading out from a continent, the floor usually begins as a continental shelf. It then drops down the continental slope, a steep descent into deeper water. Where the slope meets the deep floor, the drop eases into the continental rise, which is built from sediment cascading down the slope. Beyond it lies the abyssal plain, the main area of the seabed. Most of the ocean is very deep, and that is where the floor takes this form.

paragraphs.heading: Ridges, trenches and vents
paragraphs.text: Seafloor spreading raises mid-ocean ridges down the middle of the major ocean basins, where the floor stands a little higher than the plain around it. This mountainous rise runs through the middle of all the oceans, typically with a rift along it. Along the edges of tectonic plates lie oceanic trenches, which are deep valleys. Where plates pass over a hotspot, periodic eruptions build ridges of volcanic islands. In volcanic areas and in trenches, hydrothermal vents push very hot, high-pressure water and chemicals into the near-freezing water around them.

paragraphs.heading: Layers of depth
paragraphs.text: Deep ocean water is sorted into zones by depth, and each has its own typical salinity, pressure, temperature and life. The abyssal zone sits along the top of the abyssal plain, with its lower edge at about 6,000 m. Below it is the hadal zone, from 6,000 to 11,000 metres, which takes in the trenches and is the deepest zone of all. Depth measured down into the seabed itself, for example through a sediment core, is called depth below seafloor and is often written mbsf, for meters below the seafloor.

paragraphs.heading: Four kinds of sediment
paragraphs.text: Seabed sediments are grouped by where their material comes from. Terrigenous sediment comes from the continents, worn away by rain, rivers and glaciers or blown out to sea as dust and volcanic ash, and it is the most plentiful kind on the floor. Biogenous sediment is made of the hard parts of sea creatures, mainly phytoplankton. Hydrogenous sediment precipitates out of seawater when ocean conditions change, or forms in hydrothermal vent systems, while cosmogenous sediment comes from space. Sorted by size instead, sediment runs from fine clays and silts, together called mud, up through sand to boulders.

paragraphs.heading: A slow rain of shells
paragraphs.text: Living things help build the seabed. Phytoplankton with shells of silicate or calcium carbonate grow in great numbers near the surface. When they die, their shells sink to the floor and become part of its sediment. Microorganisms living inside the sediment also change the chemistry of the seabed.

paragraphs.heading: People and the seabed
paragraphs.text: To map the floor, ships use sound to measure water depths around the world, and submersibles help scientists study unusual seabed habitats like hydrothermal vents. People change the seabed too. Much of the world's plastic travels down waterways into the ocean, and some of it sinks to the bottom. Deep sea mining goes after valuable minerals in sulfide deposits, and dredging takes sand from shallow areas for construction and beach nourishment.
